title.en: Cane Joints Full of Lice: The Tribute of the Disabled Poor
title.zh: 裝滿蝨子的竹節:貧弱者的貢賦

region.zh: 大蘇尤各村(象徵性標記)

texts.period: Written by Garcilaso de la Vega (Inca), publ. Markham trans. 1871

source.work: Garcilasso de la Vega (El Inca), First Part of the Royal Commentaries of the Yncas, trans. C. R. Markham, London 1871

summary.en: Another sort of tribute was imposed upon those who could not work, and were called poor: at certain intervals they had to deliver a specified number of cane joints full of lice to the governor of their village. They say that the Yncas imposed this tribute in order that no one (except those exempted from tribute) should contribute nothing, however poor he might be; and therefore from those who were disabled from paying tribute in personal service was exacted a tribute of lice. It was also said that the chief reason of the Yncas for requiring this tribute was a loving care for these poor people, that they might be obliged to clean themselves, and not become a prey to the lice. For such thoughtful care as this the Yncas were called the Friends of the Poor. The Decurions were expected to see that this tribute was paid.
summary.zh: 另一種貢賦加於不能勞作、被稱為「貧者」的人:他們須定期向村中長官繳交一定數量、裝滿蝨子的竹節。相傳印加王立此貢,是為使任何人——除非免貢之人——縱然赤貧,也不致一無所獻;故對無力以勞役納貢者,便徵「蝨貢」。又有一說:印加王設此貢,本出於對貧民的體恤,使他們不得不清潔自身,免遭蝨害。因有此等細緻入微的關懷,印加王被稱為「貧者之友」。十戶之長(十夫長)負責督察此貢的繳納。

sensitivity.note: Garcilaso's most tender anecdote of Inca social policy; read with his own apologetic purpose in mind.

title.en: The Stones and Bushes Turned to Men: Garcilaso's Skeptical Pururaucas
title.zh: 石與灌木化為人形:加爾西拉索筆下的普魯勞卡斯

region.zh: 庫斯科附近亞瓦爾-潘帕(象徵性標記)

texts.period: Written by Garcilaso de la Vega (Inca), publ. Markham trans. 1871

source.work: Garcilasso de la Vega (El Inca), First Part of the Royal Commentaries of the Yncas, trans. C. R. Markham, London 1871

summary.en: The Yncas, being a people who strove to magnify their deeds by fables and false pretensions, seeing these new friends (the reinforcements), resolved not to lose the occasion, but to turn it to advantage as was their custom. They cried out that the very stones and bushes of the plain were turning into men, and coming to fight in the service of the Prince, because the Sun and the god Uiracocha had so ordered it. The Chancas, being a credulous people, were much amazed by this fable; and afterwards it was believed by all the common people throughout that empire, as Father Friar Geronimo Roman says: 'So that the field remained in the power of the Ynca. To this day all the Indians declare, in speaking of this famous battle, that the stones in the plain turned into men to fight for them, and that all this was done by the Sun to fulfil the promise that he had given to the brave Pachacuti Ynca Yupanqui.' Garcilaso, quoting Acosta's account, adds that from the time of that victory Uiracocha was held to be the universal lord; that the prince announced to his soldiers that they had not conquered their enemies, but that the victory had been gained by certain bearded men sent by the Uiracocha who were visible to none but himself, and that they had afterwards been turned into stones: they collected a great quantity of stones near the mountains which he selected, took them to the war with much devotion, holding that victory was certain with their assistance, and called them Pururaucas. Yet Garcilaso corrects the record: the Indians never had more than two gods, which were Pachacamac, who was invisible and unknown, and the Sun, who was visible and notorious; they held that Uiracocha and the other Yncas were children of the Sun.
summary.zh: 印加人素有以神話浮誇誇大戰功之風;見到援兵到來,便照例抓住時機,大肆利用。他們高喊:平原上的石頭和灌木叢都變成了人,奉太陽與維拉科查之命,來為王子助戰!昌卡人性喜輕信,聞之大駭;此後全帝國的平民也都信以為真——赫羅尼莫·羅曼神父記道:「至今所有印第安人談起這場著名會戰,仍說平原上的石頭化為人形為他們作戰,這一切都是太陽為履行他對英勇的帕查庫提·印加·尤潘琪的許諾而行的。」加爾西拉索又引阿科斯塔:自那場大捷之後,維拉科查被尊為至高之主;王子向將士宣布,此勝非人力所取,而是維拉科查所遣的、唯有王子能見的鬚髯神兵所建,戰後神兵化為石頭——人們於是拾取他所點的山邊巨石,奉為瓦卡,虔誠地抬上戰場,相信有神石相助則必勝,稱之為「普魯勞卡斯」。但加爾西拉索糾正道:印加人自來只有兩位神——隱而無名的帕查卡馬克,與顯而有名的太陽;維拉科查與歷代印加王,皆只是太陽的兒子。

sensitivity.note: The mestizo historian explicitly frames the pururaucas as an Inca propaganda invention while preserving the belief record - a uniquely critical native-voiced version.

title.en: The Field of Blood: Eight Hours at Yahuar-pampa
title.zh: 血野:亞瓦爾-潘帕八小時血戰

region.zh: 昌卡地亞瓦爾-潘帕(象徵性標記)

texts.period: Written by Garcilaso de la Vega (Inca), publ. Markham trans. 1871

source.work: Garcilasso de la Vega (El Inca), First Part of the Royal Commentaries of the Yncas, trans. C. R. Markham, London 1871

summary.en: The battle, having been so hardly won and having lasted for eight hours, was very bloody. The Indians declare that, besides the blood that was shed on the ground, a dry bed of a stream that crossed the plain also flowed with blood; hence the plain was called from that time forward Yahuar-pampa, which means 'the field of blood.' More than 30,000 Indians died, 8000 on the side of the Ynca, and the rest belonging to the nations Chanca, Hanco-huallu, Uruinarca, Vilca, Untun-sulla, and others. The two rebel masters of the camp, and the general Hanco-hualla, were made prisoners.
summary.zh: 此役得之極難,酣戰八小時,血染沙場。印第安人相傳:除了灑在地面上的鮮血,那片平原上乾涸的河床也流滿了血;自此這片平原便名為「亞瓦爾-潘帕」——血野。死者逾三萬:印加一方八千,餘者屬昌卡、安科-瓦尤、烏魯伊納爾卡、維爾卡、溫通-蘇利亞諸族。叛軍的兩位統帥與主將安科-瓦利亞俱被生擒。

sensitivity.note: Yahuar-pampa is the standard Garcilaso name for the decisive Chanca battlefield (Yuncaypampa in other sources).

title.en: Drinking with the Sun: Evaporation as the God's Draught
title.zh: 與太陽對飲:蒸發即神飲

region.en: Temple of the Sun, Cuzco (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 庫斯科太陽神廟(象徵性標記)

texts.period: Written by Garcilaso de la Vega (Inca), publ. Markham trans. 1871

source.work: Garcilasso de la Vega (El Inca), First Part of the Royal Commentaries of the Yncas, trans. C. R. Markham, London 1871

summary.en: For these Yncas, although they held the Sun to be god, treated him as if he had been a man like themselves. Among other things that they did to him in his supposed character of a man was to drink with him, and they poured the Sun's drink into a half tinajon of gold, which they placed in the court where they held their festivals, or in the temple. They declared that what appeared to be gone had been drank by the Sun, and they said truly, for the Sun's heat had evaporated the liquor. They also put out plates of meat that the Sun might eat. And when a great event happened, like this victory, they sent a special messenger to tell the Sun what had happened, and to offer up thanks to him. In accordance with this ancient custom, the prince Uiracocha Ynca sent a messenger to the Sun with the news of the victory, and with orders to the priests to get together those who had fled, that they might offer up thanksgivings and make new sacrifices. He sent another messenger to the virgins dedicated to the Sun, with the news of the victory which had been granted in return for their prayers and merits.
summary.zh: 印加人雖奉太陽為神,卻像對待族人一般與他相處。其中一樁,便是與太陽對飲:他們把太陽的酒漿倒入一只半人高的金缸,安放在舉行節宴的庭院或神廟之中;眾人眼中「消失不見」的酒,便算是太陽飲下的——他們這話倒也不假,因為那正是太陽的熱力把酒蒸發了。他們還擺上肉盤,請太陽進食。凡遇大事——如這場大捷——便遣專使向太陽報喜致謝。照這古禮,維拉科查·印加王子遣使赴太陽神廟報捷,並命祭司召集逃散之人回來謝恩獻祭;另遣一使往太陽的貞女處報喜——說這場勝利是報答她們的祈禱與功德。

sensitivity.note: The famous evaporation anecdote - the most-quoted passage of Garcilaso; his rationalist wink inside the ritual description.

title.en: The Blood-Omen Fulfilled: The Dethroned King Keeps His Yellow Fringe
title.zh: 血兆應驗:廢王仍戴黃纓

region.en: Rumi-colca palace, between Muyna and Quespicancha (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 穆伊納與基斯皮坎恰之間的魯米-科爾卡宮(象徵性標記)

texts.period: Written by Garcilaso de la Vega (Inca), publ. Markham trans. 1871

source.work: Garcilasso de la Vega (El Inca), First Part of the Royal Commentaries of the Yncas, trans. C. R. Markham, London 1871

summary.en: The prince returned to the city, put aside the yellow fringe, and adopted the red one. But though he wore the red fringe himself, he never would consent that his father should leave it off, caring little for the outward insignia, so long as he possessed the reality of dominion and power. As soon as the palace was finished it was supplied with servants and all other necessaries, so that, except the government of the kingdom, the Ynca Yahuar-huaccac was deprived of no other thing. The poor king passed the rest of his life in this solitude, deprived of his kingdom by his own son. The Indians say that this dethronement was prognosticated by the evil omen of his having wept blood in his childhood. They also say, reasoning amongst themselves and recalling the memory of past events, that if this Ynca, when he began to fear the disposition of his son, had resorted to the remedy of giving him a little poison (according to the custom of tyrants, which was practised by the sorcerers in some of the provinces of that empire) he would not have been dethroned. Others, defending the conduct of the prince, say that if his father had fallen into the hands of the enemy still worse would have befallen him. Others, who were held to be religious, said that even if the use of poison had been possible, all his predecessors would rather have died than have used it.
summary.zh: 王子回到城中,摘下黃纓,改用紅纓。然而他自己雖戴紅纓,卻始終不許父親摘下黃纓——在他看來,只要實權在握,外在的徽記無足輕重。宮殿一成,僕從用度俱全;除了失去國政,廢王亞瓦爾-瓦卡克別無所失。可憐的老王在這片幽居中度過餘生——江山斷送在親生兒子手上。印第安人說,這場廢立早有預兆:他幼年泣血的凶兆,如今應驗了。人們私下議論:這位印加王若在察覺兒子野心之初,便用上那劑小小的毒藥——暴君之間的慣技,帝國某些省份的巫師確曾使用——便不會遭此下場。另一些人為王子辯護:若老王落入敵手,下場只會更慘;棄城而逃者,性命、江山、子孫基業都將不保。還有些信教虔誠的人說:縱使毒計可行,歷代先王寧死也不肯用毒。

sensitivity.note: The wept-blood omen fulfilled; the fringe colours as rank semiotics; the poison debate is Garcilaso's moral commentary in native voices.

The poor king passed the rest of his life in this solitude, deprived of his kingdom by his own son.
